excerpt: Corporate CFOs and facility controllers need an auditable general-ledger worksheet to compare a full-time 40-hour in-house custodian against fixed-fee commercial janitorial proposals. This capex and opex template breaks down every statutory tax, workers' compensation code, equipment depreciation schedule, and consumable line item required for an accurate pro-forma analysis.

blocks.text: How to Structure a CFO-Grade Pro-Forma for a Full-Time 40-Hour Custodian

When a facility manager proposes converting an outsourced janitorial service contract into a full-time 40-hour in-house custodian position, corporate finance teams routinely reject informal memos that only compare the custodian's base hourly pay against the contractor's monthly invoice. A CFO-ready capex template full time 40 hour custodian model must separate costs into four distinct accounting buckets: Direct W-2 Gross Payroll (2,080 annual hours), Statutory & Benefits Burden (GL Payroll Taxes & Insurance), Non-Productive Leave Backfill (208 paid off-floor hours), and Capital Equipment & Chemical Opex.

Crucially, your pro-forma must also harmonize the calendar math. Commercial janitorial contracts bill on a 52-week annual cycle divided across 12 months—equaling 4.33 weeks per month (21.65 weekday visits per month for a 5x-weekly scope). In-house hourly payroll, meanwhile, posts biweekly across 26 pay periods (80 hours per check, 2,080 hours per year). Converting both schedules to a standardized 12-month and per-square-foot ledger prevents the common 8.3% four-week budgeting error.

blocks.title: Class 9014 Workers' Compensation & Liability Audit Rule
blocks.text: Do not apply your clerical office workers' compensation rate (NCCI Class 8810, typically $0.12–$0.25 per $100 of payroll) to an in-house custodian. Insurance auditors reclassify full-time custodial staff under NCCI Class 9014 (Buildings—Operation by Contractors) or Class 9015 (Buildings—Operation by Owner), which carries a rate of $3.80 to $6.50 per $100 of payroll—a 20x higher premium multiplier.

blocks.text: Unlike an outsourced contractor who arrives on Day 1 with commercial vacuums, mobile carts, mop buckets, and safety signage already amortized across dozens of client buildings, an in-house custodial launch requires an immediate capital outlay of $4,200 to $6,800. In a Class A office environment, selecting durable, high-efficiency rolling and receptacle gear prevents premature replacement and cuts daily labor minutes:

items: Daytime Executive Caddy (Rubbermaid Commercial Executive Quick Cart Large): For daytime touch-ups in glass-walled lobbies and boardrooms where an open mop cart looks intrusive, this Teflon-coated charcoal caddy carries a 60 lb capacity on quiet casters with a stealth executive look and removable compartment dividers.

Mobile Waste Barrel Organizer (Rubbermaid Commercial Brute Rim Caddy Attachment): Snapping directly onto the rim of a 44-gallon Brute trash barrel, this 9-compartment rim caddy holds spray bottles, wet floor signs, safety glasses, and liner rolls on integrated tool clips—turning a bulk waste collector into a self-contained mobile workstation.

Architectural Breakroom & Restroom Receptacles (Simplehuman 55L / 14.5-Gal Commercial Semi-Round Open Can): Upgrading high-traffic coffee bars and restroom exits to brushed stainless steel 14.5-gallon semi-round cans with heavy bases and lift-off lids ensures ADA-friendly wall clearance and speeds liner changes without exposed plastic overhang.

blocks.text: Hidden General Ledger Costs Most In-House Worksheets Miss
Even detailed spreadsheets frequently omit four indirect expenses that hit the corporate P&L when custodial management is internalized:

items.name: Recruiting, Drug Screening & Turnover Friction ($1,200–$2,400 per cycle)
items.text: When a full-time custodian resigns, HR spends 15 to 25 hours posting job ads, conducting interviews, verifying I-9 eligibility, running criminal background checks, and onboarding. In an industry with 75%+ annual turnover, budget at least 0.75 replacement cycles per year.

items.name: Management & Quality Inspection Time (2.5 hrs/week)
items.text: With an outsourced vendor, the facility manager spends 30 minutes per month reviewing KPI scorecards with the vendor's account manager. With an in-house W-2 custodian, the office or facility manager becomes the direct supervisor—approving timecards, resolving attendance issues, ordering chemical refills, and auditing restroom quality for 2.5 hours every week ($5,200/yr in allocated managerial salary).

items.name: Quarterly Deep Floor Care Subcontracting ($0.03–$0.06/sq ft/month)
items.text: A solo 40-hour custodian cannot strip and recoat 5,000 sq ft of VCT vinyl or hot-water extract 18,000 sq ft of carpet tiles alone while keeping up with daily trash and restrooms. You must still carry a $675 to $1,350/month accrual ($8,100–$16,200/year on 22,500 sq ft) for quarterly specialty floor contractors.

items.name: General Liability & Slip-and-Fall Deductible Exposure
items.text: Outsourced janitorial vendors carry $1M/$2M Commercial General Liability (CGL) policies naming the property owner and tenant as Additional Insureds. If an in-house custodian leaves a wet tile floor unmarked and a visitor slips, the claim hits your company's primary liability policy and deductible directly.

blocks.text: CFO Decision Checklist: Should You Approve a Full-Time 40-Hour Custodian Req?
Before signing an internal headcount requisition for a full-time 40-hour custodian, verify that your facility meets at least three of the four financial justification criteria below:

blocks.title: The $1,400/Month Daytime Value Offset Rule
blocks.text: Because a full-time 40-hour W-2 custodian costs roughly $2,400 to $2,800 per month more than an outsourced evening cleaning contract on a 20,000–25,000 sq ft office, the in-house requisition only achieves positive ROI if the employee performs at least 15 to 20 hours per week of daytime facility maintenance, conference catering resets, or security-cleared support that would otherwise cost $1,400 to $2,800/month in third-party handyman or porter bills.
Plug your facility's exact square footage, flooring mix, and local wage rates into our Office Cleaning Cost Calculator to generate an instant outsourced benchmark for your CFO worksheet.

faqs.q: How should startup janitorial equipment capex be amortized in a CFO budget worksheet?
faqs.a: Commercial cleaning hardware—including HEPA backpack vacuums, high-capacity janitorial carts, walk-behind 20-inch micro-scrubbers, and commercial Brute/Slim Jim waste stations—typically carries a 36-month (3-year) straight-line depreciation life in facility operating budgets, plus a 10% annual maintenance allowance for belts, brushes, filters, and caster replacements.

faqs.q: Why must a 40-hour custodian budget include 160 to 208 hours of temporary backfill labor?
faqs.a: A full-time W-2 employee paid for 2,080 hours per year typically receives 80 hours of federal holidays, 80 hours of paid vacation, and 48 hours of paid sick time (208 total non-working hours). Because office restrooms and breakrooms still require daily sanitation when the custodian is on vacation or out sick, facilities must budget temporary agency or on-call vendor coverage at $35 to $55/hr for at least 160 of those hours.

faqs.q: What is the standard consumable cost per square foot to enter in a janitorial budget?
faqs.a: When budgeting restroom and breakroom consumables (paper hand towels, bath tissue, foaming hand soap, and LLDPE can liners), use our national benchmark of $0.012 to $0.025 per square foot per visit—or roughly $0.26 to $0.54 per square foot per month for a densely occupied office serviced 5 days per week (21.65 visits/month).

faqs.q: Does an in-house custodian eliminate the need for a quarterly floor care budget?
faqs.a: Rarely. Unless the facility purchases $4,500+ in dedicated carpet extractors and low-speed rotary buffers AND pays overtime for weekend project work, one 40-hour custodian is fully consumed by daily trash, restroom disinfection, and routine floor vacuuming/mopping. Most facilities still budget $0.03 to $0.06/sq ft/month for quarterly outsourced floor restoration.
